$comment: COACH ME, rebuilt 2026-09-11 on his complaint that there was not much there he could use. The
twelve checks of 2026-08-22 were sound and sourced; what was missing was any link to his own swims
and a way to read one at the side of the pool. Now the tab opens on what his lengths say (derived
on the page, from the stroke counts inside his last long pieces), then the checks grouped by where
in the swim they matter, each one a Do line and a Check line with the source's own words under it.
SOURCES ARE US MASTERS SWIMMING ONLY, his ruling of 2026-09-02. Two were added today: the open
turns guide, because his stops happen at the wall, and the breathing drills article, whose one
sentence quoted here puts the hum in US Masters' own words. Its hypoxic drills are deliberately
NOT used: plan.json's breathing cue forbids every 4 or 5 on the continuity piece, for the reason
written in its stop cue. Every quote is checked against content/swim/sources/ by validate.mjs.
The history of every earlier check, including three tests that were inverted or unperformable,

items.name: Count your strokes on every length
items.do: Count stroke cycles on one arm, every length of the long piece.
items.check: A length two or more above your usual count cost more than it should have, whatever it felt like.

quotes.text: Counting your strokes is a measure of swimming efficiency. The fewer strokes you can take, the more efficiently you're swimming.

items.name: Breathe out the whole time your face is in
items.do: Let the air out slowly while your face is down. Hum it.
items.check: The hum runs until your mouth clears the water, and your first move there is to breathe in, not out.

quotes.text: You should exhale while your mouth is underwater and inhale when it's out of the water.
Exhale as you swim, letting air out slowly as if you're humming.

items.name: Turn without standing up
items.do: Touch with one hand, knees to your chest, roll back, feet on the wall, twist off it as you push.
items.check: Eight walls in a row without a foot on the floor, on an easy swim, before you use it in the long piece.

quotes.text: Open turns for freestyle are like open turns for butterfly and breaststroke in terms of how to do them. The only difference is that you only use one hand to touch the wall instead of two.
The most important movement in an open turn is aggressively bringing your knees to your chest and then rolling backward.
As you push off, twist off the wall, just as if you were going to jump and twist on land while jumping up.
Don't use your turns as an opportunity to rest; instead, use them as an opportunity to gain an advantage.

items.name: Arrive on a full stroke
items.do: Adjust your stroke three or four cycles out so you reach the wall on a full stroke.
items.check: You touch on a full reach, with no glide in and no short chopped stroke.

quotes.text: Start adjusting your stroke three or four cycles from the wall to ensure you hit the wall on a full stroke.

items.name: Legs low: press the chest down first
items.do: If your legs ride low, press your head and chest down before you try kicking harder.
items.check: Kick harder and nothing changes: it is not the kick. Press the chest and see whether the legs rise.

quotes.text: The first strategy is to press your head and chest, the lighter end of the seesaw, down into the water.

items.name: Keep the lower back and hips firm
items.do: Hold tension through the lower back and hips.
items.check: Push off and glide with no kick: count how long before the legs drop. Longer over the weeks is the line improving.

quotes.text: Your lower back and hips are key for creating tension in the back of your body. This tension holds your legs up at the surface of the water, preventing them from sinking.

items.name: Small, fast kick
items.do: Keep the kick small and quick, feet under the surface.
items.check: No air on the soles of your feet.

quotes.text: Kicking is expensive. It takes a lot of energy to produce speed with your legs, and a big kick takes a lot more energy than a smaller kick.

items.name: The kick starts at the hip
items.do: Hip first, knee second, ankle third.
items.check: You cannot see this from inside the water. A phone on the deck filming one length is the only way to know.

quotes.text: Your down-kick begins at your hip, your knee moves second, and your ankle moves third.

items.name: Bend the elbow before you pull
items.do: From the stretch, drop the hand down and in as the elbow bends out to the side.
items.check: One length with tight fists, one with open hands. Barely slower on fists means the forearm is already doing the work.

quotes.text: drop your hand down and in from the outstretched position while your elbow bends, pointing out to the side.

items.name: Finish every pull past the hip
items.do: Push the water all the way back until your hand passes your hip.
items.check: Your hand brushes your thigh before it leaves the water.

quotes.text: your hands should finish your pull just past your hips. Your arm should not be completely straight at this point.

items.name: Rotate hips and shoulders together
items.do: Turn the whole spine as one, not the shoulders alone.
items.check: If your count climbs on the side you breathe to, the rotation is not even.

quotes.text: Rotation only works if you keep your spine relatively straight. Your whole spine needs to rotate in the same way at the same time for your rotation to fulfill its function.

sources.label: US Masters Swimming: Drills for your freestyle breathing pattern
